finding.claim: /transfer never checks that amount is positive. A negative amount passes the balance check and reverses the transfer, so the attacker debits the victim and credits themselves. The victim must be an existing account key in BAL. No consent from the victim is needed.

trace.note: amount taken from request.json with no type or sign validation
BAL[g.user] < amount is False for a negative amount, so the guard passes
BAL[to] += (-X) decreases the victim's balance, possibly below zero
/withdraw does have an amount <= 0 check, which makes the missing check in /transfer clear. The attacker can then withdraw the stolen funds.

finding.guards_checked: Only BAL[g.user] < amount (bank.py:11). No sign check, no type check, and no recipient consent. The code never sets g.user, so authentication has to come from elsewhere. None is visible in this repo.

verdict.guard_found: Only `BAL[g.user] < amount` at bank.py:11, which a negative amount passes. No sign/type check, no consent check. Authentication is not visible, since g.user is never set in this repo, and bank.py is the only file. /withdraw has an `amount <= 0` check at bank.py:21, but /transfer has none.
verdict.reason: bank.py:10-14 takes `amount` from the JSON body with no sign check, so a negative value passes `BAL[g.user] < amount` at line 11. Line 13 then credits the caller and line 14 debits the victim, and bank.py:21 shows /withdraw checks `amount <= 0` where /transfer does not. The attacker only needs to be an authenticated low-privilege user, and the missing authentication in this file does not block the attack.

verdict_facts.guard_found: Only the balance check `BAL[g.user] < amount` at bank.py:11. It has no sign or type check and no recipient consent. /withdraw has `amount <= 0` at bank.py:21, but /transfer does not. g.user is set by upstream middleware, which the maintainer says is trusted.
verdict_facts.reason: At bank.py:11 a negative amount makes `BAL[g.user] < amount` False, so lines 13-14 run and move funds from an existing victim account to the attacker. The only attacker requirement is being an authenticated user, and no control blocks it. The trace lines all match, including the `amount <= 0` check at bank.py:21 in /withdraw.

finding.claim: /withdraw and /transfer both do a check-then-act on the balance with no lock or atomic operation. Concurrent requests can all pass the balance check before any debit lands, so the attacker withdraws or transfers more than they hold (double-spend). Flask's dev server is threaded by default, and WSGI servers run multiple workers or threads. With multiple processes each worker has its own BAL, which is a separate consistency bug.
finding.source: Many parallel authenticated POST /withdraw or /transfer requests, each with amount equal to the full balance

trace.note: The debit is a separate non-atomic read-modify-write. Another thread can pass the check in between.
The same pattern is in /transfer, and the debit at line 13 is likewise not atomic with the check.

finding.guards_checked: No threading.Lock, no database transaction, no atomic compare-and-set. BAL is a plain module-level dict.

verdict.reason: bank.py:21 checks BAL[g.user] < amount and bank.py:23 debits it separately (same pattern at bank.py:11/13), with no lock or transaction, so concurrent requests from an authenticated user can overdraw. The race window is narrow under the GIL, and multi-process deployments make BAL inconsistent anyway.

verdict_facts.reason: bank.py:21 and bank.py:11 check BAL[g.user] and bank.py:23 and bank.py:13 debit it as a separate read-modify-write, with no lock, transaction, or atomic operation, so any authenticated user can race concurrent requests. The window is narrow under the CPython GIL but real, since thread switches can occur between bytecodes.

finding.claim: Python's JSON parser accepts the non-standard literals NaN and Infinity. With amount=NaN, every comparison is False, so both the `<= 0` check and the `BAL < amount` check pass. The debit makes the attacker's balance NaN. After that, every `BAL[g.user] < amount` check is False, so the attacker can withdraw or transfer any amount without limit. The attacker needs no funds, and the sole precondition is an existing account.
finding.source: Authenticated user's raw JSON body: {"amount": NaN}. Flask's request.json accepts this.
finding.sink: BAL[g.user] -= amount (bank.py:23) leaves the balance as NaN. Later withdrawals then bypass the balance check (bank.py:21).

trace.note: amount = request.json["amount"] is not type-checked, so it can be a float NaN
nan <= 0 is False and BAL < nan is False, so the abort is skipped
BAL becomes NaN. Every later BAL < amount check is False, which gives unlimited withdrawals.

finding.guards_checked: Only `amount <= 0 or BAL[g.user] < amount`. There is no isinstance check, no math.isfinite check, and no integer or Decimal enforcement. The same applies to /transfer at bank.py:11.

verdict.guard_found: none (only `amount <= 0 or BAL[g.user] < amount` at bank.py:21; no type, isfinite, or Decimal check; no before_request or validation in the file)
verdict.reason: At bank.py:20-23, amount=NaN from request.json makes both comparisons at line 21 False, so `BAL[g.user] -= amount` sets the balance to NaN, and every later `BAL[g.user] < amount` check is False, so any withdrawal passes; the same flaw exists in /transfer at bank.py:11.

verdict_facts.guard_found: Only `amount <= 0 or BAL[g.user] < amount` at bank.py:21 (and `BAL[g.user] < amount` at bank.py:11). Both are float comparisons that are False for NaN. No type or isfinite check, no auth decorator in this file.
verdict_facts.reason: At bank.py:20-23, amount=NaN (accepted by Flask's json.loads) makes `nan <= 0` and `BAL < nan` both False, so abort is skipped. BAL[g.user] becomes NaN at bank.py:23, and every later `NaN < amount` check is False, so withdrawals are unlimited. Any authenticated user with an account can do this.
